Vatutin then secretly shifted Rybalko's 3rd Guards Tank Army north, across the river and through marshy ground, into the Lyutezh bridgehead above the city. The attack opened on 3 November behind a massive bombardment, broke the German line and swung south. Soviet troops entered Kiev in the night of 5–6 November, the eve of the anniversary of the Revolution.

They found a city wrecked and largely emptied of its people. At Babi Yar on the outskirts, where more than 33,000 Jews had been shot in September 1941, the SS had used prisoners in August and September 1943 to dig up and burn the bodies of its victims, to hide the evidence.
significance: The fall of Kiev breached the Dnieper line and opened the way into right-bank Ukraine; a German counter-attack retook Zhitomir in November but could not recover the city.
uncertaintyNote: The wider Kiev offensive lasted until 13 November; the end date here marks the liberation of the city.
sources: David M. Glantz and Jonathan M. House, When Titans Clashed (1995)
Karel C. Berkhoff, Harvest of Despair: Life and Death in Ukraine under Nazi Rule (2004)
Richard Overy, Russia's War (1997)

title: Battle of Tarawa
place: Betio island, Tarawa Atoll, Gilbert Islands (Kiribati)

strength.focus: c. 4,700 men, including c. 1,200 Korean labourers
strength.opponent: c. 18,000 Marines in the 2nd Marine Division

casualties: US c. 1,000 killed and c. 2,100 wounded; Japanese and Korean c. 4,600 dead, with only 17 Japanese and 129 Koreans taken alive
summary: US Marines storm the tiny, heavily fortified island of Betio. Landing craft stranded on the reef, they wade ashore under fire, and take it in 76 hours of brutal fighting.
detail:
The invasion of the Gilberts opened the Central Pacific drive towards Japan. Betio, a flat coral island less than 3 km long, was defended by Japanese naval infantry in concrete and coconut-log bunkers around its airfield.

On 20 November a heavy naval and air bombardment failed to destroy the defences. A low tide left too little water over the fringing reef for the landing craft, so only the first waves in tracked amphibious tractors crossed to the beach; later waves had to wade hundreds of metres through the lagoon under machine-gun fire, and the losses were terrible. By nightfall the Marines held only a shallow strip along the sea wall, but the Japanese, their communications wrecked and their commander Shibasaki apparently killed, did not counter-attack effectively.

Over the next two days the Marines, with tanks and reinforcements, worked through the bunkers with explosives and flamethrowers. A final Japanese charge on the night of 22–23 November was broken, and the island was declared secure on 23 November. Almost the entire garrison died.
significance: Tarawa's shocking cost forced major improvements in amphibious technique, from more amphibious tractors to underwater demolition teams and better bombardment, that were applied in every later Pacific landing.
uncertaintyNote: Figures for the garrison and its Korean labourers vary slightly; the circumstances of Shibasaki's death are uncertain.
sources: Joseph H. Alexander, Utmost Savagery: The Three Days of Tarawa (1995)
Ronald Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
Ian W. Toll, The Conquering Tide (2015)

title: Tehran Conference
place: Soviet embassy, Tehran, Iran

sides.focus: Germany and the Axis (the subject of the talks)
sides.opponent: Soviet Union, United States and Britain

summary: Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill meet together for the first time. They fix the invasion of France for May 1944, and Stalin promises to enter the war against Japan once Germany is beaten.
detail:
The 'Big Three' met in Tehran, in an Iran occupied since 1941 by Soviet and British troops. Roosevelt, invited to stay at the Soviet embassy for security, used private talks with Stalin to build a relationship, sometimes at Churchill's expense.

The central decision was military. Stalin pressed hard for a firm date for the long-promised second front, and Churchill's preference for further operations in the Mediterranean and the Balkans was set aside: Operation Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion, was fixed for May 1944, supported by a landing in southern France, and Stalin undertook to launch a major offensive at the same time. He also confirmed that the Soviet Union would join the war against Japan after Germany's defeat.

On Poland, the leaders informally agreed that its eastern border should follow roughly the Curzon Line, with compensation from Germany in the west, without consulting the Polish government in exile. In a ceremony, Churchill presented Stalin with a sword from King George VI honouring the defenders of Stalingrad.
significance: Tehran fixed the strategy that would end the war in Europe and set the pattern of the post-war settlement, including the shifting of Poland's borders, later confirmed at Yalta.
uncertaintyNote: No Axis party took part; the focus slot names the powers against which the strategy was set.
sources: Gerhard L. Weinberg, A World at Arms (1994)
Richard Overy, Why the Allies Won (1995)
S.M. Plokhy, Yalta: The Price of Peace (2010)
